author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

text:
AI has no common sense. I asked it to wire up the DUT in the testbench, it got the sanity testcase passing, but it left some ports opened. No even an intern would make this mistake.

I can explicitly tell it to check for floating signals, and it would get it right, but who knows what other common sense AI is lacking.

author.name: Dan B.
author.headline: Seasoned Electrical/FPGA/ASIC/RTL Engineer with individual & managerial experience

comments.text: Did you try saying "make sure all inputs and outputs are exercised and tested by the test bench"? If any issues are encountered, ask for clarification.

author.name: Horace Chan

replies.text: Dan B. Nope. But I don't have to tell my intern that too. AI suppose to be smarter than an intern.

author.name: Paul Marriott
author.headline: 1st, Senior Principal Verification Engineer at NXP

replies.text: Horace Chan some things are so "obvious" that they're not written down. I have had heated discussions with requirements architects on this subject:) The tl;dr version is that everything should be in the requirements, even things that everyone "knows" to be obvious - because if it's not written, it can't be verified nor traced.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text: Paul Marriott Do you know that a standard/spec leave out little "obvious" things on purpose, it is a barrier of entry. The companies with engineers in the committee working on the draft knows those subtle decisions, so their product will be 100% compatible. The newcomer who doesn't know those subtle things can only get 99.9% working and the last 0.1% is the moat.
